big: Before paying ₹20,000 to a 'stock adviser', Rohan spent two minutes on the regulator's website. The name was not there. He kept his ₹20,000.

lines: Who has time to check everyone who calls me?
Only check before you pay or share something. It takes minutes, and the habits are few: look it up, use the official app, add a second step, and call back yourself.

title: Verify before you trust
stops: Look up an adviser on the regulator's official list
A link sent by message is as safe as the official app
A second sign-in step protects you if a password leaks
Calling the number the caller gives is a good check
caps: A registration check takes minutes, and the list is public.
Type the official address or use the app, never a link from a stranger.
Two-factor sign-in adds a step that a thief does not have.
Call back on the number printed on your card or on the official site.

rows: Search the regulator's list for the adviser, broker or fund
Type the address or open the app. Skip links from strangers
Turn on the second step for broker and bank logins
Hang up, and call the printed official number yourself
note: For advisers and brokers, the SEBI website lists registered names. Banks print official numbers on cards and statements.

q: Meena is asked to pay a person for stock advice. What should she do first?
opts: Ask for a screenshot of his past profits
Pay a small amount to test him first
Check the regulator's list for his name
Check how many people follow him online
why: Screenshots are easy to fake, so they prove nothing about the person.
Even a small payment can start a longer fraud and is not a check.
The regulator's list shows whether the person may legally give such advice.
Followers can be bought, so their number proves nothing.

q: A message with a link says Rohan's broker account needs an update. What is the safe step?
opts: Click the link to finish the update quickly
Reply with his login details at once
Forward the link to a friend to test it out
why: Using the official app or a typed address avoids fake look-alike pages.
Clicking the link may take him to a fake page that steals his details.
Login details given in a reply go straight to the fraudster.
Forwarding the link puts his friend at risk and checks nothing.

q: Why switch on two-factor sign-in for a broker account?
opts: It makes the password quite unnecessary
It speeds up every trade he makes
It lowers the brokerage that is charged
why: The password is still needed, and the second step comes on top of it.
A second step, such as a code, blocks a thief who has only the password.
It adds a step, so it does not make trades faster.
Brokerage charges are not affected by security settings.

q: A caller claims to be from Meena's bank and asks for details. What is the best check?
opts: Call back the number the caller gives her
Ask him to send an email with the request
Give half of the details now, half later
Hang up, and call the printed number
why: A number given by the caller may lead straight back to the fraudster.
An email can be forged as easily as a call, so it proves nothing.
Half the details can still be used, so none should be shared.
She picks the number herself, so she reaches the real bank.

pts: Check the regulator's list before you pay any adviser.
Use the official app or a typed address, never a stranger's link.
Turn on two-factor sign-in, and call back on the printed number yourself.
